variants.title: The bookshop that refused to die
variants.text:
When Margaret Hale took over a small bookshop in York in 1998, everyone told her she was making a mistake. Online shopping was growing fast, and independent bookshops were closing all over the country. "People said I was throwing my money away," she remembers.

Twenty-five years later, Hale's Books is still open, and it is believed to be one of the most successful independent shops in the north of England. What is the secret? "Books are not just products," Margaret explains. "Reading is about connection. The connection between a reader and a bookseller who knows them is something an algorithm can't copy."

Although sales fell during the first years, she refused to give up. She organised readings, book clubs and a café, and gradually the shop became a meeting place. In 2020, when the shop had to close for months, customers had been ordering books by phone for weeks before she even set up a website.

Despite her success, Margaret is modest. "If my husband hadn't supported me, I wouldn't be here today. And if I were a better businesswoman, I'd probably be rich, but I wouldn't be happy."

Last year the shop was featured in a TV documentary, and visitors now come from all over the world. Margaret still works behind the counter six days a week. "Retire? Over my dead body," she laughs.

variants.title: Music on the ward
variants.text:
Ten years ago, the cellist Tom Ellis was playing in one of London's best-known orchestras. Then his daughter became seriously ill, and he spent months sitting in a children's hospital. "Silence is the hardest thing in a hospital," he says. "The silence at night, when nobody knows what will happen."

One evening, he brought his cello into the ward. "I had been playing for about ten minutes when a nurse came in. I thought she was going to tell me to stop. Instead, she sat down and cried."

That night was the beginning of Music on the Ward, a charity which is now said to visit more than sixty hospitals a year. Although the musicians are all professionals, nobody is paid. "We do it because it works," Tom explains. "Doctors have told us that children sleep better after a concert."

His daughter, who is now a healthy teenager, sometimes joins him. "If she hadn't been ill, I would still be in the orchestra, and I'd never have discovered what music can really do."

Last spring the charity's work was turned into a radio series, and donations have tripled since then. Not bad, as Tom says, for "a man with a cello who couldn't sleep".

options: Tom went back to the orchestra.

options: He doesn't like the radio series.
